title: State v. Jacques
description: Whether the trial court violated the defendant's constitutional right to a second probable cause hearing, abused its discretion by admitting a prior inconsistent statement from a witness with memory loss, and abused its discretion by admitting unreliable jailhouse informant testimony.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the trial court correctly denied a second probable cause hearing, properly admitted Jenkins' statement as a prior inconsistent statement, and reasonably found Vazquez's testimony reliable, asserting no constitutional violations or abuse of discretion.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court violated his constitutional right to a second probable cause hearing, infringed his confrontation clause rights by admitting Jenkins' statement, and abused its discretion by admitting unreliable jailhouse informant testimony.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of conviction, upholding the trial court's decisions on all three issues raised by the defendant.

title: State v. Michael Sharpe
description: Whether the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of an individual's shed DNA from discarded items, without consent or a warrant, constitutes an unreasonable invasion of privacy under the state and federal constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of the defendant's shed DNA was constitutional, as the DNA was discarded, and the testing was solely for identification purposes in a criminal investigation, thus not violating privacy rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the warrantless extraction and testing of his shed DNA from discarded items, without probable cause or a warrant, constituted an unreasonable invasion of his privacy under both state and federal constitutions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, ruling that the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of his shed DNA from discarded items did not violate his privacy rights.

title: State v. McFarland
description: Whether the thirty-two year interval between the murders and the defendant's arrest violated his due process rights under the Connecticut constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the conviction should be affirmed and the prearrest delay did not violate the defendant's due process rights, asserting legitimate investigative justifications for the delay.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the thirty-two year prearrest delay violated his due process rights under the Connecticut constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the conviction of the defendant, ruling that the thirty-two year interval between the murders and the defendant's arrest did not violate his due process rights.

title: State v. Haynes
description: Whether illegally obtained statements that are merely inconsistent with a defendant's trial testimony, as opposed to directly contradictory, should be admissible for impeachment purposes under the state constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued for a broader application of the impeachment exception, allowing the use of any inconsistent statement obtained in violation of Miranda rights to impeach a defendant's trial testimony, aligning with federal precedent.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued for a more nuanced exclusionary rule under the state constitution, limiting the use of illegally obtained statements for impeachment only to those that are directly contradictory to trial testimony, not merely inconsistent, to prevent perjury and uphold constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled with the State, adhering to the federal rule that allows illegally obtained statements to be used for impeachment if they are inconsistent with the defendant's trial testimony, even if not directly contradictory.

title: State v. King
description: Whether a defendant's waiver of a jury trial is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary if the trial court fails to explain that a three-judge panel, unlike a jury, does not require a unanimous decision for a guilty verdict.
plaintiff_argument: The state implicitly argued that the defendant's jury trial waiver was knowing, intelligent, and voluntary, and that the trial court's canvass was sufficient despite not explicitly explaining the non-unanimous nature of a three-judge panel verdict.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that her jury trial waiver was not knowing, intelligent, and voluntary, and thus unconstitutional, because the trial court failed to explain that a three-judge panel could reach a guilty verdict by a majority vote, unlike a unanimous jury verdict.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the defendant's conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, ruling that trial courts must explicitly inform defendants waiving a jury trial for a three-judge panel that a majority verdict is sufficient, but declined to extend the prohibition on presubmission deliberations to three-judge panels.

title: Spillane v. Lamont
description: Whether the doctrine of sovereign immunity bars a declaratory judgment action challenging the constitutionality of a statute that eliminated the religious exemption to school vaccination requirements.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that P.A. 21-6 violates their constitutional rights to free exercise of religion, equal protection, and a free public education, and that a statutory waiver of sovereign immunity applies.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the state is immune from suit under sovereign immunity, and that the plaintiffs' claims do not satisfy the exceptions to this doctrine.
decision_outcome: The court reversed in part and affirmed in part the trial court's judgment, concluding that the plaintiffs' constitutional claims (free exercise, equal protection, and right to education) failed as a matter of law and were barred by sovereign immunity, despite finding that a statutory waiver of immunity for free exercise claims against legislation exists.

title: Tatum v. Commissioner of Corrections
description: Whether the principles set forth in Guilbert and Dickson regarding eyewitness identification apply retroactively to the petitioner's case on collateral review.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that both Guilbert and Dickson announced watershed rules of criminal procedure that should apply retroactively, or alternatively, that justice requires their retroactive application to his case because they overruled specific holdings in his direct appeal.
defendant_argument: The respondent contended that neither Guilbert nor Dickson applies retroactively, citing a footnote in Dickson that stated the new constitutional rule did not apply retroactively on collateral review.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Court's judgment, ruling that the principles of Dickson (regarding unduly suggestive in-court identifications) apply retroactively to the petitioner's case, but Guilbert (regarding expert testimony on eyewitness identification) does not. The case is remanded for a new trial on the relevant counts.

title: State v. Avoletta
description: Whether Special Act 17-4, which allowed the defendants to refile a previously dismissed claim against the state for injuries from poor indoor air quality in public schools, constitutes an unconstitutional public emolument in violation of the Connecticut constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that Special Act 17-4 is an unconstitutional public emolument because it grants an exclusive private benefit without a legitimate public purpose, as the state was not responsible for the defendants' procedural default in filing their claim.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Special Act 17-4 serves legitimate public policy purposes, such as providing compensation for injuries, ensuring safe school settings, holding government officials accountable, and allowing full adjudication of similar claims, and therefore is not an unconstitutional public emolument.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Court's judgment, ruling that Special Act 17-4 is an unconstitutional public emolument because it does not serve a legitimate public purpose.

title: State v. Langston
description: Whether a trial court can properly consider conduct related to a charge of which a criminal defendant was acquitted, when sentencing the defendant on other charges of which the defendant was convicted.
plaintiff_argument: The sentencing court's consideration of conduct related to a charge of which he was acquitted violated his rights to due process and a trial by jury under both federal and state constitutions.
defendant_argument: The practice of considering acquitted conduct during sentencing is permissible under established federal and state precedent, and the sentence imposed was within the statutorily prescribed range for the counts of conviction.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to correct an illegal sentence.

title: State v. Qinxuan Pan
description: Whether the trial court abused its discretion in setting a $20 million bond and incorrectly denying the defendant's request for a 10 percent cash bail option.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant argued that the $20 million bond was unreasonably high and a functional denial of bail, and that the trial court incorrectly concluded it lacked the authority to grant a 10 percent cash option.
defendant_argument: The state contended that the $20 million bond was reasonable given the defendant's extreme flight risk and public safety concerns, and did not challenge the trial court's conclusion regarding the 10 percent cash option.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the $20 million bond amount as a reasonable exercise of discretion but found that the trial court incorrectly determined it lacked discretion to consider a 10 percent cash bail option, remanding the case for that consideration.

title: State v. Graham
description: Whether the trial court erred in admitting an accomplice's statement and whether the prosecutor committed impropriety during closing arguments, thereby violating the defendant's confrontation rights and right to a fair trial.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the accomplice's statement was properly admitted as a statement against penal interest, the prosecutor's tailoring arguments were specific and permissible, and the claims regarding cooperation agreements were unpreserved evidentiary claims.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court erred in admitting the accomplice's statement as inadmissible hearsay and a violation of confrontation rights, and that the prosecutor's generic tailoring arguments and use of cooperation agreements constituted impropriety.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Connecticut affirmed the judgment of conviction, finding no error in the trial court's decisions regarding the admission of evidence or the prosecutor's arguments.

title: In re Annessa J.
description: Whether the virtual termination of parental rights trial violated the respondent mother's constitutional rights to an in-person trial and confrontation, and whether the Appellate Court correctly expanded the legal standard for posttermination visitation.
plaintiff_argument: The virtual trial did not violate Valerie's constitutional rights, and the Appellate Court improperly expanded the standard for posttermination visitation beyond "necessary or appropriate" to secure the child's welfare.
defendant_argument: Valerie argued the virtual trial violated her state constitutional right to an in-person trial and her federal due process right to confront witnesses. Both respondents argued the trial court applied an incorrect legal standard for posttermination visitation, and the Appellate Court correctly broadened it to include the child's "best interest."
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the termination of parental rights, finding no constitutional violation in the virtual trial, and reversed the Appellate Court's expansion of the standard for posttermination visitation, reinstating the "necessary or appropriate" standard.

title: State v. Morel-Vargas
description: Whether a defendant's waiver of their right to testify in a criminal trial must be personally asserted on the record, or if defense counsel's representation combined with the defendant's silence is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The state argues that the defendant himself does not need to affirmatively articulate his waiver of the right to testify on the record; it can be inferred from defense counsel's in-court representation combined with the defendant's silence.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the constitution requires him to affirmatively inform the trial court, either orally or in writing, that he is waiving his right to testify, and that counsel's representation with his silence is insufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of conviction, concluding that defense counsel's in-court representation and the defendant's silence satisfied the constitutional requirement for a valid waiver, but prospectively mandated new procedures for trial courts to ensure such waivers are knowing, intelligent, and voluntary.

title: State v. Correa
description: Whether Article first, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution prohibits the police from conducting a warrantless canine sniff of the exterior door to a motel room and a warrantless visual sweep of the room for the purpose of detecting illegal drugs.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that a warrantless canine sniff of a motel room door is not a search under the state constitution, or if it is, it only requires reasonable articulable suspicion, and that the visual sweep was justified by exigent circumstances or the independent source doctrine.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that a warrantless canine sniff of the motel room door and a warrantless visual sweep of the room violated his rights under Article first, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution, requiring a warrant based on probable cause.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Court's judgment, concluding that a warrantless canine sniff of a motel room door is an unlawful search requiring a warrant and that the visual sweep was not justified by exigent circumstances, remanding the case for the state to present evidence on independent source and inevitable discovery doctrines.

title: State v. Bemer
description: Whether the trial court's order for sexually transmitted disease and HIV testing of the defendant, based solely on being charged with a sexual offense, violates the defendant's constitutional right to be free from unreasonable searches, with the plaintiff arguing the statute broadly authorizes such testing and the defendant arguing it requires a finding of clear and imminent danger or compelling need.
plaintiff_argument: The state and victims argued that General Statutes § 54-102a (b) broadly authorizes HIV testing when a defendant is charged with an enumerated sexual offense, without requiring the stringent 'clear and imminent danger' or 'compelling need' standard from § 19a-582 (d) (8), and that the statute is constitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court abused its discretion by ordering HIV testing without a finding of 'clear and imminent danger' and 'compelling need' as required by General Statutes § 19a-582 (d) (8), which he contended is incorporated into § 54-102a (b), and that the statute otherwise violates his state constitutional rights against unreasonable searches.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order for sexually transmitted disease examination and HIV testing and remanded the case for a new hearing, requiring the trial court to find that such testing would provide useful, practical information to a victim that cannot reasonably be obtained otherwise.

title: Anthony A. v. Commissioner of Corrections
description: Whether the Department of Correction violated the petitioner's constitutional rights to procedural and substantive due process, and his state constitutional right against punishment not warranted by law, by classifying him as a sex offender based on non-conviction information and without adequate procedural protections.
plaintiff_argument: The Department of Correction violated his procedural due process rights by denying him the opportunity to call witnesses, failing to provide adequate notice of evidence, and lacking an impartial decision-maker for his appeal. It also violated his substantive due process rights and state constitutional right against unwarranted punishment by classifying him as a sex offender without sufficient evidence and proper process.
defendant_argument: The Department of Correction followed proper procedures, had sufficient evidence to classify the petitioner as a sex offender based on non-conviction information, and did not violate his constitutional rights. The classification was rationally related to legitimate penological interests.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the habeas court's judgment, finding that the Department of Correction violated the petitioner's procedural due process rights under both federal and state constitutions, and his state constitutional right under article first, § 9, by classifying him as a sex offender without proper procedural protections. The case was remanded to issue a writ of habeas corpus and expunge the petitioner's sex treatment need score.

title: Fay v. Merrill
description: Whether Governor Ned Lamont's Executive Order No. 7QQ, which added COVID-19 as a permissible reason for absentee voting, violates article sixth, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Executive Order No. 7QQ was unconstitutional because the governor lacked the authority to expand absentee voting, and the constitutional term 'sickness' does not include a general pandemic like COVID-19 but rather individual illness.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that the legislature's ratification of Executive Order No. 7QQ rendered the separation of powers claim moot, and that the constitutional term 'sickness' is broad enough to encompass a specific disease like COVID-19, not just an individual's personal illness.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that Executive Order No. 7QQ does not violate article sixth, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution, as the legislative ratification mooted the separation of powers claim and 'sickness' includes the COVID-19 pandemic.
